newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - Sharp jump in SAfrica Jan M3, credit down.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Sharp jump in SAfrica Jan M3, credit down.

text.p: Foreign capital inflows this year would inflate January South African M3 money supply although analysts differed on what amount of upward pressure would be brought to bear on the closely watched indicator.
They also said an expected sharp rise in the year-on-year number would be a statistical abberation and growth in the monetary aggregates should slow sharply from February.

The markets will be flooded with a host of data this week starting with January trade data on Tuesday, followed by January CPI, fourth quarter GDP growth and preliminary data for January M3 money supply and private sector credit extension growth on Thursday.
Eleven economists polled by Reuters forecast a sharp jump in M3 money supply growth but a slight easing in credit demand growth.

The consensus forecast was for M3 year-on-year growth of 15.8 percent from 13.7 percent in December with a wide forecast range of between 12.5 percent and 18.1 percent. Private credit is seen expanding 15.3 percent against 15.75 percent with a range of between 14.5 percent and 15.9 percent.
The data is due at 1500 GMT on Thursday.

"The big variable is the large amount of foreign money that came in so it depends to what extent that has been taken out of the market...the increase in M3 could therefore be 15.5 percent or maybe 16.2 percent," said ING Barings economist Hania Farhan.
Central bank governor Chris Stals told financial market players at a local "road show" this week that capital inflows would impact on M3, but noted that a lot of the inflows were short-term.
The counterpart to the inflows was the reduction of bank credit extension and the central bank would use some of the inflows to reduce its forward book.

Stals reiterated at a number of public platforms the importance of a restrictive monetary policy to bring down the rate of increase in bank credit extension and in the money supply to head off the risk of inflation.
With higher inflation still a serious threat, money supply growth would have to be capped at 10 percent this year - a guideline the country should be able to meet, he said.
Another reason for the sharp increase in M3 growth would be an exceptionally low year ago comparative base, economists said.
They said private sector credit growth normally showed a subdued growth rate in January and it appeared that high interest rates were beginning to bite.

"In general, we're looking for the trend (in credit extension) to be downwards," Rand Merchant Bank treasury economist Julia Roy said, adding there was scope for cut in official interest rates later in the second quarter.
After an undertaking by Stals this week to renew the fight against inflation, the January CPI numbers will be keenly watched.
Stals stressed that inflation remained a major threat to the monetary authorities and the challenge was to prevent an escalation in inflationary expectations.

The consensus forecast of the eleven economists polled was for a year-on-year inflation rate of 9.2 percent from 9.4 percent in December, and a month-on-month increase of 1.1 percent compared to 1.0 percent.
The data is due for release at 1100 GMT on Thursday.
Standard Bank's economics unit expected the year-on-year rate to fall slightly because of a high base in January 1996.
Expected contributors to the monthly rise were the housing and medical care categories and transport as a result of a fuel price and some car price increases.
It noted, however, that the CPI weightings would change from January and this could substantially affect the forecast.
The majority of economists polled expected CPI to peak just under 10 percent at around 9.8 percent in the second quarter.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
